# On the Strange Beauty of Incomplete Things

I've been thinking lately about unfinished sentences. You know the ones—they trail off mid-thought, suspended in white space, leaving the reader to fill in the gaps. There's something peculiarly honest about them. They suggest that not everything needs wrapping up, that ambiguity isn't always a failure of communication but sometimes its most perfect expression.

This thought came to me while I was looking at my bookshelves, at all the books I've started but never finished. I used to feel guilty about these half-read volumes, stacked horizontally atop the finished ones like a monument to my own incompetence. Why couldn't I just commit? Why did I start Moby Dick four separate times across four different decades? But recently I've made peace with it. Some books, I think, are meant to be kept incomplete. They exist in my life as perpetual possibilities rather than resolved narratives, and there's something beautiful in that.

We're obsessed with completion in ways that seem almost pathological. We finish what we start. We close the loops. We want narrative arcs that resolve, projects that conclude, conversations that reach understanding. I understand the impulse. There's a satisfaction to completion that's almost physiological—that sense of a task accomplished, a box checked, a weight set down. We are creatures who crave closure.

But I wonder if we've lost something in this relentless drive toward finished things. I think about medieval cathedrals, built across centuries, their architecture and ornamentation evolving with changing styles and sensibilities. The Sagrada Família in Barcelona has been under construction since 1883. Most of the people who began it died never seeing it finished. Yet it stands as one of the most magnificent structures humanity has created, and perhaps it's magnificent partly *because* it remains incomplete, because it refuses the finality of conclusion.

Or consider scientific understanding. We talk about scientific facts as though they're finished products, perfect little boxes of knowledge. But that's a profound misunderstanding of how science works. Every answer opens new questions. Every solved mystery spawns a dozen new mysteries. The entire enterprise would collapse if we achieved total completion. Science is beautiful precisely because it's infinite in its incompleteness, because there will always be something else to discover, some new frontier pushing back the darkness.

I've been reading about Japanese aesthetics lately, and I keep coming back to the concept of *ma*—negative space, the space between things. In art, architecture, music, and design, there's this deep understanding that what you don't show is as important as what you do. That silence between musical notes is as much part of the composition as the notes themselves. The empty space in a painting is an active component, not a failure to fill the canvas.

There's also *wabi-sabi*, which encompasses an appreciation for impermanence, imperfection, and the incomplete. A cracked tea bowl, weathered by use and time. A poem that cuts off abruptly. A garden that's allowed to decay in beautiful ways. There's a tenderness in this aesthetic that Western perfectionism doesn't easily accommodate. It accepts that things break, that beauty doesn't require flawlessness, that incompleteness might be closer to truth than any finished product could be.

I think about my own life this way increasingly. I'm in my thirties now, and I don't know if that's more than halfway through or not even close. I certainly don't have life "figured out" in any comprehensive way. I'm still learning how to be a person. I still make mistakes I thought I'd graduated from making. I still wrestle with self-doubt and uncertainty. And increasingly, I'm okay with this. Not in the toxic-positivity way of "embrace the journey, man," but in a deeper sense: I'm okay with being an incomplete work.

There's a temptation to see one's thirties as a deadline—by this age you should have your career established, your relationships secured, your personality finalized. But what if that's the wrong framework entirely? What if the goal isn't to reach some finished state of "adulthood" but to remain perpetually in motion, perpetually growing, perpetually uncompleted?

I have a friend who's been working on the same novel for eight years. When I asked him when he'd finish it, he looked slightly offended. "I don't want to finish it," he said. "I like who I am as a person while I'm writing it. When I finish it, I'll be someone else, and I'm not sure I want to know who that person is." I thought he was joking, but I don't think he was. There's something wise in that resistance to completion.

The fear underneath productivity culture, I think, is the fear that once we've finished everything on our list, once we've achieved everything we've set out to achieve, we'll have to confront the fundamental emptiness of existence. So we keep adding to the list. We gamify our lives. We turn everything into a project to be managed. What if we stopped?

I've been thinking about habits this way too. We talk about building good habits and breaking bad ones, as though our behavioral lives are construction projects. But what if habits are more like gardens? You plant something, and it grows, and it spreads, and sometimes it thrives in unexpected ways and sometimes it withers. You don't build a garden and then finish with it. You're always tending it, always in relationship with it, always learning from it.

My mother has been doing the same crossword puzzle, on and off, for three years. It's a crossword in a hardcover book, not a newspaper, so it won't degrade or disappear. She works on it when she's waiting for coffee to brew or during a lunch break. She's maybe a third of the way through it. I asked her if she's trying to finish it, and she said, "Not particularly." She just likes the activity, the way it focuses her mind. Finishing would be beside the point.

There's something about incompleteness that preserves possibility. A finished meal becomes memory; a meal in the midst of being eaten is present experience. A finished conversation is history; an ongoing conversation is actual relationship. A finished life—well, we don't really know what that looks like, but we fear it.

Incompleteness is also more honest about the nature of meaning-making. We act as though meaning exists in the world waiting to be discovered, like facts about geology or biology. But meaning is something we create, something we generate through our engagement with things. A novel isn't finished when the author writes the final word; it's finished when a reader reads it, and then finished again when another reader reads it, differently, in the light of their own life. Meaning is infinitely incomplete.

I think about all the things I've wanted to learn and abandoned halfway through. Piano lessons from age seven to twelve. Spanish, which I attempted to learn in college and high school and casually and seriously. Drawing classes. Photography. Programming. At one time, I felt ashamed of this scattered incompleteness, this lack of mastery. Now I'm not sure. I can play a few songs on the piano. I can conduct basic conversations in Spanish. I can see the world partially through a photographer's eye. I can understand code well enough to read other people's and roughly understand what's happening.

Is this failure? Or is it a kind of literacy? A sampling of different ways of being in the world, different modes of perception? I don't regret any of them for being incomplete. I think they've all become part of how I think and see and move through the world.

There's an essay by Annie Dillard where she talks about how living is not something most people are good at. It's something people do, mostly badly, while thinking about other things. We're all fundamentally incomplete at this central task. We're all amateurs at being alive. There's a strange comfort in that—if we're all stumbling through this more or less incompetently, maybe the goal isn't to achieve some kind of mastery but just to show up, to pay attention, to be as present as we can manage in the midst of our confusion.

I've been rereading some David Foster Wallace essays, and he keeps returning to the idea that life is fundamentally about attention—about learning to direct your consciousness deliberately rather than having it directed for you by habit, fear, and desire. But notice what he doesn't claim: that you'll ever achieve perfect attention, complete clarity, full presence. You won't. You're always going to be partial, limited, incomplete in your awareness. The practice isn't about reaching a finished state of enlightenment but about the practice itself.

Incompleteness is also, I think, a prerequisite for compassion. When you're incomplete, when you don't have everything figured out, you extend grace to others who are similarly lost. When you admit your own brokenness, you can hold space for others' brokenness. Perfection is isolating. Completeness is lonely. We connect through our gaps.

I think of the kintsugi technique in Japanese pottery, where broken ceramics are repaired with gold seams. The breaks don't disappear; they're highlighted, integrated, made into part of the beauty. That seems like a good way to move through the world—not trying to hide the places where we've broken or failed or remained incomplete, but acknowledging them as part of our actual shape.

There's a line in Leonard Cohen's "Anthem" that keeps coming back to me: "There is a crack in everything / That's how the light gets in." Not: there shouldn't be cracks. Not: you should fix the cracks. The cracks are essential. They're how light penetrates the darkness. They're how growth happens. They're what keeps us open.

As I write this, I'm aware that I haven't said anything terribly original. The imperfection of things, the value of incompleteness, the problem with perfectionism—these are not new insights. But maybe that's the point. Maybe these truths need to be repeated endlessly because we keep forgetting them, keep slipping back into the pursuit of completion and closure and certainty.

Let me end this essay incompletely. Let me trail off without a neat conclusion, without having tied everything together or resolved all the tensions I've raised. Let me leave you with unfinished thoughts floating in white space.

Because maybe that's more honest. Maybe that's how we actually live—in fragments, in pieces, in ongoing becoming. Not working toward some finished version of ourselves or our understanding, but perpetually in the process of becoming, perpetually incomplete, perpetually open to what comes next.

And maybe that's not a failure or a tragedy. Maybe that's the only life worth living.
